title: English Vocabulary in Use — Pre-intermediate and Intermediate · Units 61–62
description: Curated vocabulary and spoken forms for numbers, dates, calculations, distance, physical dimensions and size.
sourceNotice: Prepared from user-supplied reference pages. Vocabulary targets follow the source topics; example sentences and teaching notes are newly written. Source exercises, extended passages, and illustrations are not reproduced.

audit.scope: Teaching sections, figures, exercises and relevant answer-key entries checked for vocabulary and construction coverage.
audit.pronunciation: Broad British IPA for short targets and source-indexed entries; connected speech and accent variants are not exhaustively represented. Optional IPA may be blank if a reliable transcription was not established.
audit.languagePolicy: All content is in English except Portuguese translations under pt.
audit.reviewMethod: Teaching and practice pages and illustrations inspected; answer key compared; editorial checks of numerical readings, measurement collocations, British English and translations; static audio checks and JSON serialization round trip.
audit.limitations: Live VocabLab browser importer, speech synthesis, and speech-recognition tests were not available.

units.title: Unit 61 — Numbers
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Pre-intermediate and Intermediate (4th Edition); printed pages 128–129 (PDF pages 129–130).
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Pre-intermediate and Intermediate (4th Edition)
learningObjectives: Read cardinal numbers naturally in British English and distinguish exact from general quantities.
Say dates, ordinals and calendar years using appropriate British-English patterns.
Pronounce and interpret fractions, decimal numbers and percentages.
Describe basic calculations using add, subtract, multiply and divide constructions.
Choose natural spoken forms of zero in telephone numbers, decimals and temperatures.

items.example: The town has three hundred and seventy-nine registered volunteers.
items.note: The British-English reading of 379 includes and after hundred.

items.word: two thousand, eight hundred and sixty
items.example: The venue has two thousand, eight hundred and sixty seats.
items.note: Reads 2,860; thousand is singular after a specific number.

items.pt: cinco mil e oitenta e quatro
items.example: We counted five thousand and eighty-four entries.
items.note: Reads 5,084; no hundreds are present in the final group.

items.example: The region has about four hundred and seventy thousand residents.
items.note: Reads 470,000; thousand has no final -s in an exact number.

items.example: The video reached two million views.
items.note: Use million without -s after a specified number.

items.example: The estimate is close to three billion pounds.
items.note: In modern English, billion means one thousand million.

items.example: A hundred people signed the letter.
items.note: Exact numbered amounts use two hundred, not two hundreds.

items.example: Three thousand tickets were sold.
items.note: Specific cardinal numbers take thousand without a plural ending.

items.example: One million people watched the programme.
items.note: Specific cardinal numbers take million without a plural ending.

items.example: That is a billion times larger than the original figure.
items.note: A cardinal unit equal to one thousand million.

items.example: Thousands of people waited in the rain.
items.note: Use the plural and of for an unspecified large number.

items.example: Millions of insects live in the forest.
items.note: An approximate quantity rather than an exact number.

items.example: Hundreds of people took part in the survey.
items.note: Use the plural and of for a general quantity.

items.example: The centre has two thousand, five hundred members.
items.note: Do not put and immediately after thousand when a full hundred follows.

items.example: The hall seats two hundred and twenty people.
items.note: British English commonly includes and between the hundreds and tens.

items.example: There were two hundred and twenty guests altogether.
items.note: Means in total; appears in the number correction exercise.

items.example: The exhibition opens on the fourth of June.
items.note: Spoken form for 4 June; use the ordinal, not four.

items.example: My appointment is on June the fourth.
items.note: Alternative British spoken order for 4 June.

items.example: The presentation will be on the twenty-first of May.
items.note: Spoken form for 21 May; twenty-first is ordinal.

items.example: The course starts on May the twenty-first.
items.note: Month-first alternative for saying this date.

items.example: The results will be released on the seventh of April.
items.note: Use seventh, not seven, when speaking a date.

items.example: They got married on the tenth of September.
items.note: Spoken form of 10 September in an exercise.

items.example: Her contract ends on the thirty-first of August.
items.note: Use the ordinal thirty-first for the day.

items.pt: mil novecentos e noventa e sete
items.example: The company was founded in nineteen ninety-seven.
items.note: A common way to say the year 1997.

items.example: She graduated in two thousand and sixteen.
items.note: One possible way to say the year 2016.

items.example: The project started in twenty sixteen.
items.note: An alternative way to say the year 2016.

items.pt: mil novecentos e noventa e seis
items.example: My older brother was born in nineteen ninety-six.
items.note: Common reading of 1996 in the practice exercises.

items.example: They met in twenty twelve.
items.note: An accepted way to read the year 2012.

items.example: The word seventh is an ordinal number.
items.note: Ordinal numbers identify order, including days of the month.

items.example: The journey took one and a quarter hours.
items.note: Spoken fraction 1¼; the book contrasts it with 1.25.

items.example: We need one and a half litres of water.
items.note: Spoken fraction 1½; note the singular half.

items.example: The meeting lasted one and three quarters of an hour.
items.note: Spoken fraction 1¾; quarters is plural.

items.example: The cable measures one point two five metres.
items.note: Spoken decimal 1.25; read each digit after point separately.

items.example: The container holds one point five litres.
items.note: Spoken decimal 1.5.

items.example: The shelf is one point seven five metres wide.
items.note: Spoken decimal 1.75; digits after point are said one by one.

items.example: They spent two and a half hours on the train.
items.note: Practice target for 2½.

items.example: The amount was nought point two five grams.
items.note: British reading of 0.25; zero is read nought.

items.example: The reading was ten point oh four volts.
items.note: Reading of 10.04: oh is one possible name for the zero digit.

items.example: Write a decimal point between the whole number and the fraction.
items.note: A written dot that is spoken as point in decimal numbers.

items.example: One half is a simple fraction.
items.note: A way to represent a part of a whole.

items.example: About twenty-six per cent of the class were absent.
items.note: British written form per cent; follows a number.

items.example: The majority of voters supported the change.
items.note: More than half of a group.

items.example: Only a small minority disagreed with the decision.
items.note: Less than half of a group in this comparison.

items.example: The vast majority of participants completed the course.
items.note: A very large proportion, much more than half.

items.example: A small minority opposed the new rules.
items.note: A small share of the whole group.

items.example: Forty-seven per cent of respondents chose the first option.
items.note: Reads 47% in the unit exercises.

items.example: Addition helps us find the total.
items.note: The mathematical process of combining amounts.

items.example: Subtraction tells us how much remains.
items.note: The mathematical process of taking one amount from another.

items.example: The next exercise involves multiplication.
items.note: The process of multiplying numbers.

items.example: We used division to find the answer.
items.note: The process of dividing one amount by another.

items.example: Seven plus three equals ten.
items.note: The standard word for the addition sign.

items.example: Nine minus four is five.
items.note: Used for subtracting and for negative numbers.

items.example: Six times seven is forty-two.
items.note: Natural spoken alternative to multiplied by.

items.example: Eight multiplied by seven is fifty-six.
items.note: Verbal form for multiplication; also used in an exercise.

items.example: Sixty-five divided by thirteen is five.
items.note: Verbal form for division.

items.example: Six plus four equals ten.
items.note: Links an operation to its result.

items.example: Could you add up these figures for me?
items.note: Often followed by numbers or an amount.

items.example: I cannot work out the answer without paper.
items.note: Here work out means calculate or find an answer.

items.example: I get stuck when a calculation has too many steps.
items.note: Means reach a point where you cannot continue.

items.example: We need to calculate the total cost.
items.note: Work out an answer using mathematics.

items.example: Check your calculation before sending the report.
items.note: A mathematical process or its written result.

items.example: Use a calculator to check the result.
items.note: An electronic device for doing calculations.

items.example: Basic arithmetic is useful for everyday shopping.
items.note: The branch of mathematics involving ordinary number operations.

items.example: The final digit of my code is zero.
items.note: Common in counting, mathematics and telephone numbers.

items.pt: zero (especialmente na leitura britânica de decimais)
items.example: The result was nought point seven.
items.note: British English name for zero, particularly in decimals.

items.example: My phone number starts with six oh three.
items.note: In telephone numbers and some decimals, oh can represent zero.

items.example: Her extension number contains double four.
items.note: Says two consecutive 4 digits in a telephone number.

items.example: It was ten degrees below zero overnight.
items.note: An alternative to minus ten degrees when discussing temperature.

items.word: nine four oh double three eight
items.pt: nove quatro zero três três oito (dígitos de telefone)
items.example: The final contact number is nine four oh double three eight.
items.note: Read the digits individually, with oh for zero and double for a repeated digit.

items.example: The temperature is twenty degrees Celsius.
items.note: A standard unit used to report temperature.

items.example: The forecast predicts minus five degrees Celsius tomorrow.
items.note: A natural spoken form for a negative temperature in the exercises.

sectionsChecked: A: Cardinal numbers and singular units after exact numbers; general plurals such as thousands of
B: Spoken dates, ordinals and years; common mistakes
D: Percentages, majority, minority and intensification
E: Addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, calculation and common verb phrases
F: Spoken zero in telephone numbers, decimals and temperatures
Exercises 61.1–61.5: readings, corrections, calculations and personalised prompts

units.title: Unit 62 — Distance, dimensions and size
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Pre-intermediate and Intermediate (4th Edition); printed pages 130–131 (PDF pages 131–132).
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Pre-intermediate and Intermediate (4th Edition)
learningObjectives: Ask about distance using how far and reply with appropriate distance expressions.
Recognise British metric and traditional imperial units of length.
Distinguish length, width, height and depth, and form natural measurement questions.
Use tall, high, deep, shallow, long and wide with suitable nouns.
Use strong and contrasting size adjectives such as huge, tiny, thick and narrow.

items.example: The distance between the towns is about twenty miles.
items.note: How far apart places or things are.

items.example: The entrance is only a metre from the pavement.
items.note: A standard metric length unit; British spelling is metre.

items.example: The gap is about one centimetre wide.
items.note: A hundredth of a metre.

items.example: The metal sheet is one millimetre thick.
items.note: A thousandth of a metre.

items.example: The station is one kilometre away.
items.note: A metric distance unit equal to one thousand metres.

items.example: There is a supermarket about a mile away.
items.note: A distance unit of about 1.6 kilometres.

items.example: The sign is fifty yards along the road.
items.note: A traditional British length unit, a little shorter than a metre.

items.example: The shelf is about one foot deep.
items.note: A length unit of roughly thirty centimetres; plural feet.

items.example: The room is twelve feet long.
items.note: Plural of foot when measuring distance or height.

items.example: The board is an inch thick.
items.note: A unit of roughly 2.5 centimetres.

items.example: The screen is fifteen inches across.
items.note: Plural of inch.

items.example: How far is the nearest supermarket?
items.note: Use how far to ask about the distance to a place.

items.example: The beach is about a mile away.
items.note: Away expresses the distance from a reference point.

items.example: The next bus stop is half a mile away.
items.note: A common spoken distance.

items.example: The nearest hospital is on the other side of town.
items.note: Superlative of near; identifies the shortest distance.

items.example: We have at least two miles left to walk.
items.note: Introduces a minimum amount or distance.

items.example: The village is a couple of miles from here.
items.note: Usually approximately two miles, possibly a little more.

items.example: It is ten minutes’ walk to the station.
items.note: Distance measured by walking time: minutes’ walk, not minutes’ walking.

items.example: The airport is a long way from here.
items.note: Affirmative distance description: it is a long way, not it is far.

items.example: The park is not far from our house.
items.note: Natural negative distance expression.

items.example: It is quite a long way to the next petrol station.
items.note: Stronger than a long way in some contexts.

items.pt: logo ali na esquina; muito perto
items.example: There is a chemist just round the corner.
items.note: An informal expression for a very nearby place.

items.example: The post office is a hundred yards up the road.
items.note: Means further along the same road; does not require an uphill slope.

items.example: There is a small café down the road.
items.note: Means further along the road; does not require a downhill slope.

items.example: The nearest hotel is about two miles away.
items.note: Precedes an approximate number or measurement.

items.example: The station is three kilometres from here.
items.note: Marks the reference point for a distance.

items.example: We need the dimensions of the storage cupboard.
items.note: Measurements such as length, width, height and depth.

items.example: The length of the table is two metres.
items.note: Noun; adjective long.

items.example: The table is two metres long.
items.note: Adjective used when describing length.

items.example: How long is the new bridge?
items.note: With physical objects, asks about length.

items.example: The width of the door is ninety centimetres.
items.note: Noun; adjective wide.

items.example: The road is wide enough for two cars.
items.note: Opposite of narrow when describing width.

items.example: How wide is the entrance?
items.note: A direct question about width.

items.example: The height of the wall is two metres.
items.note: Noun used for measurements; related to high and tall.

items.example: The mountain is over three thousand metres high.
items.note: Use high for a wall or mountain; people are usually tall.

items.example: The new building is very tall.
items.note: Used for people, trees and buildings; not normally for mountains.

items.example: How high is the garden wall?
items.note: Use high when asking about the height of a wall or mountain.

items.example: How tall is your brother?
items.note: Common question for a person’s height.

items.example: The depth of the lake varies throughout the year.
items.note: Noun; related adjective deep.

items.example: The water gets deep near the far end of the pool.
items.note: Opposite of shallow.

items.example: Children can swim safely in the shallow end.
items.note: Describes water or containers with little depth.

items.example: How deep is the swimming pool?
items.note: A direct question about depth.

items.example: Beginners should stay in the shallow end.
items.note: The part of a swimming pool with less depth.

items.example: The diving board is beside the deep end.
items.note: The part of a swimming pool with greater depth.

items.example: Stand at the other end of the table.
items.note: One of the outermost points of a long object.

items.example: The garage is five metres long.
items.note: A measured length is expressed with number + metres + adjective.

items.example: The wall is three metres high.
items.note: Use high for this measurement, rather than tall.

items.example: The pool is four metres deep at one end.
items.note: An adjective describes the dimension after the measurement.

items.example: What size table would fit in this room?
items.note: The overall dimensions or amount of space something occupies.

items.example: The manual is thick and heavy.
items.note: Opposite of thin; can describe a book or material.

items.example: This thin book fits in my pocket.
items.note: Opposite of thick for an object such as a book.

items.example: The theatre has a huge entrance hall.
items.note: A stronger adjective than big.

items.example: They live in an enormous house.
items.note: A synonym of huge; much larger than ordinary.

items.example: There is a tiny kitchen in the flat.
items.note: A strong opposite of huge or enormous.

items.example: A giant crab appeared under the rock.
items.note: Adjective for something extremely large of its kind.

items.example: Buses cannot use the narrow bridge.
items.note: Opposite of wide.

items.example: He is fairly short compared with his brothers.
items.note: The opposite of tall when discussing a person.

items.example: The family lives in a small flat.
items.note: Neutral opposite of big; tiny is much stronger.

items.example: They need a bigger meeting room.
items.note: Ordinary size adjective; huge and enormous are stronger.

sectionsChecked: A: Distances, units, and illustrated location dialogues; minutes’ walk and a long way
B: Diagrammed dimensions of a table and swimming pool; adjectives, question forms and tall/high contrasts
C: Size adjectives and lexical opposites
Exercises 62.1–62.3: opposite adjectives, measurement questions and contextual answers
